cards.front: Recall a key point about Stage Types and Performance Spaces
cards.back: Proscenium arch: audience on one side, framed stage — creates a 'fourth wall', common in traditional theatres.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Stage Types and Performance Spaces
cards.back: Thrust stage: audience on three sides — intimate, breaks fourth wall, used in Shakespeare's Globe.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Stage Types and Performance Spaces
cards.back: In-the-round: audience on all sides — most intimate, actors must keep moving to avoid backs to audience.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Stage Types and Performance Spaces
cards.back: Traverse: audience on two opposite sides — creates a catwalk/battle effect, highly dynamic.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Stage Types and Performance Spaces
cards.back: Promenade: audience moves through the space — immersive, site-specific, breaks traditional boundaries.

cards.front: What should you know about drama exam tips?
cards.back: When writing about stage types, always state the name, describe the audience-performer relationship, and explain WHY a director might choose it. Never just list features — always link to dramatic effect.
One side (e.g. Elaborate sets, controlled focus)
Three sides (e.g. Intimate, breaks fourth wall)

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: It doesn't matter what stage type you use — the audience can always see the action. Correct: Stage type fundamentally changes the audience-performer relationship and what the audience can see. In-the-round requires constant actor repositioning; proscenium allows controlled focus. Directors choose stage types deliberately to create specific effects.
A director is staging a play about imprisonment. Which stage type would best communicate this theme to the audience? Justify your choice with detailed reference to how the space would be used.

GCSE Drama has three components: Understanding Drama (40% written exam), Devising Drama (30% NEA — devised performance + portfolio), Texts in Practice (30% NEA — two performances from a script).
